sections.html: The cardinalfishes (Apogonidae) are a species-rich (ca. 370 species), mainly marine group of mostly small-bodied, mouth-breeding perch-like fish. Very well known species are the Banggai Cardinalfish (Pterapogon kauderni) and the Pyjama Cardinalfish (Sphaeramia nematoptera). Only very few species have made it into freshwater. The most important freshwater genus is Glossamia with currently 11 recognized species. Most do not grow larger than 8-10 cm, whereas the largest specimen of G. aprion ever caught measured 18 cm.

All Glossamia species originate from New Guinea and Australia. Since hardly any ornamental fishes are exported from there, and if they are, they are rainbowfishes, Glossamia remained almost unknown in the aquaristics of the western world until now.
In the wild, Glossamia often form a very substantial portion of the biomass of the waters they inhabit. The fish are attached to dense underwater vegetation.
Their diet consists of aquatic insects, crustaceans (shrimp) and small fish.

Without dense vegetation, they do not feel safe and are shy and skittish. This changes immediately when they have "herbage" in the tank. Among themselves and towards fish that do not qualify as food, they are completely peaceful. In Australia, the species has the popular name "mouth almighty".

Externally there are no visible sex differences. Initially the females were thought to be plumper and a little smaller than the males, but a brooding animal was observed that was small and fat, so apparently the smaller ones are the males, which eat themselves big and round before taking care of the brood.
As with all cardinalfish, they are mouthbrooders in the male sex.
